stops.name: Genoa, the landing of the exile
stops.campa: On 4 May 1915 he crosses the frontier and comes down to Genoa, and the crowds are already at the stations as if a sovereign travelled. Five years of exile end in flowers and delirium. The government that half-invited him is already frightened of him; the neutralist parliament holds the majority, but the piazzas from this hour belong to the poet. He sleeps little, corrects the speech, and looks out at the harbour from which the Thousand sailed. Tomorrow he will talk a kingdom into a war.

stops.name: Quarto dei Mille, the Sagra dei Mille, the speech from the rock
stops.campa: On 5 May 1915, before the bronze of Garibaldi's Thousand and a sea of twenty thousand, he preaches the new Sermon on the Mount: the beatitudes rewritten for a nation hungry for war. Blessed are the young, hungry and thirsty for glory, for they shall be satisfied. The King has stayed away; the government trembles at every clause. From the rock of Quarto the interventionist May is ignited, the radiant May, and Italy is talked toward the trenches by a poet, an event without precedent in the modern chronicles.
stops.quote: Beati i giovani che sono affamati e assetati di gloria, perché saranno saziati... O beati quelli che più hanno, perché più potranno dare, più potranno ardere.

stops.name: Rome, the balcony of the Hotel Regina
stops.campa: In Rome the radiant May boils. From the balcony of the Hotel Regina on Via Veneto he harangues the crowds night after night, naming the neutralist Giolitti a traitor, calling for the parliament of the old Italy to be swept into the Tiber. The city answers with torchlight processions. Ministers consider arresting him and discover it is no longer possible: the crowd has become an organ of his voice. The technique of the balcony, the sacred dialogue of Comandante and piazza, is founded here, and others are watching who will use it for twenty years.

stops.name: Rome, the Campidoglio oration
stops.campa: On the Capitoline, navel of the Latin world, he gives the last and greatest of the May orations, unsheathing the sword of Nino Bixio before the crowd. Rome above him, Rome beneath him: he speaks as if the she-wolf herself had retained counsel. Within the week the Chamber capitulates, full powers are voted, and on 24 May Italy enters the war. The poet has his war; the war, though it does not know it yet, has its poet: fifty-two years old, half-blind with ambition, demanding a uniform.

stops.name: Over Trieste, the first flight of the poet-aviator
stops.campa: On 7 August 1915, lieutenant of the Novara Lancers seconded to the air, he flies with Giuseppe Miraglia over unredeemed Trieste and lets fall not bombs but messages weighted with ribbons: courage, brothers, the end of your patience is near. The Austrians answer with anti-aircraft fire; he notes the black flowers of the bursts with a connoisseur's calm. The war of the poet-aviator begins: every mission a canto, every city a stanza to be liberated. Miraglia, the beloved pilot, has four months to live.

stops.name: Grado, the forced landing, the eye given to the war
stops.campa: On 16 January 1916 the seaplane returning from Grado strikes the water hard and the poet's temple strikes the machine-gun butt. He flies again within days, hiding the wound; when the doctors finally look, the right eye is lost, the retina detached, the left threatened. The omen is read aloud by destiny: the seer half-blinded, like every seer of the old stories, at the exact price of second sight. He accepts the tariff without bargaining and asks how soon a one-eyed man may fly.

stops.name: Venice, the dark room of the Casetta Rossa, Notturno on paper strips
stops.campa: In the little red house on the Grand Canal he lies bandaged in the dark, head lower than his feet, forbidden to move, forbidden light. His daughter Renata, Sirenetta, cuts ten thousand strips of paper, one line wide, and on these cartigli, blind, he writes the Notturno: the sounds of Venice at war coming across the water, the dead pilots visiting the dark room, memory operating like sonar. The prose of a sightless man becomes the newest in Italian. Even mutilation, the canon observes, he converts into an instrument.
stops.quote: Ho gli occhi bendati. Sto supino nel letto, col torso immobile, col capo riverso... Scrivo sopra una stretta lista di carta che contiene una riga.

stops.name: The mouth of the Timavo, Randaccio's flag
stops.campa: With the infantry now, he carries a tricolour meant to be raised over Duino and marches with Major Giovanni Randaccio on the night attack at the Timavo: the river of the Argonauts, the river with the underground course, the most mythological water on the front. The attack breaks; Randaccio takes his death-wound and dies with the flag for a pillow. The poet brings the bloodied banner back and will sleep beneath it at the Vittoriale for twenty years. The Timavo enters his personal liturgy: where the river goes under the rock, the friend went under the earth.

stops.name: Over Cattaro, the long night raid
stops.campa: In the night of 4-5 October 1917 he rides a bomber of the San Marco squadron across the whole Adriatic to the Bocche di Cattaro, the deep fjord where the Austrian fleet sleeps behind its mountains. Hours over open sea, engines against the bora, the bombs laid into the anchorage, and the return at dawn. He is fifty-four years old and the youngest man on the raid by his own account. The Adriatic, he repeats, is a gulf and the gulf is Italian: the war of the poet is a cartography lesson delivered by air.

stops.name: Bakar, the Beffa di Buccari, thirty of one fate
stops.campa: In the night of 10-11 February 1918 three tiny MAS torpedo boats slip forty miles up the enemy's own gulf into the bay of Buccari and loose their torpedoes among the anchored shipping. The material damage is nothing; the wound to Austrian pride is immense. Before withdrawing, the poet sets three sealed bottles afloat, dressed in tricolour ribbons, each carrying his mockery in ink. Out of the raid comes the song, thirty of one fate, and thirty-one with death, and the motto he coins for the MAS: Memento audere semper.
stops.quote: In onta alla cautissima Flotta austriaca... sono venuti col ferro e col fuoco a scuotere la prudenza nel suo più comodo rifugio i marinai d'Italia, che si ridono d'ogni sorta di reti e di sbarre, pronti sempre a osare l'inosabile.
stops.quote_source: Message sealed in the bottles of Buccari, 10-11 February 1918

stops.name: San Pelagio, dawn of the Vienna flight
stops.campa: At 5:50 in the morning of 9 August 1918, from the field of San Pelagio near Padua, eleven SVA biplanes of the 87th Squadriglia La Serenissima lift off for Vienna: a thousand kilometres over the Alps, at the extreme edge of fuel and possibility. The poet rides in the modified two-seater, fifty-five years old, one-eyed, forbidden the mission by every authority and obeyed by none of them. Seven machines will hold the course. On the fuselages, the lion of Saint Mark; in the lockers, fifty thousand leaflets in his hand and three hundred fifty thousand in Ojetti's plainer prose.

stops.name: Vienna, the leaflets over the enemy capital
stops.campa: At 9:20 the tricolour wing appears over Vienna. No bombs: paper. The leaflets spiral down onto the Graben and the Stephansplatz: we could be dropping tonnes of explosive, they say; we drop instead a three-coloured greeting, the three colours of liberty. Viennese crowds look up at the impossible Italians strolling the sky of the Habsburg capital. Not a shot rises. The squadron turns home with empty racks and full glory, and the war of the poet reaches the form it was always seeking: an air raid composed entirely of rhetoric.
stops.quote: In questo mattino d'agosto, mentre si compie il quarto anno della vostra convulsione disperata e luminosamente incomincia l'anno della nostra piena energia... VIENNESI!
stops.quote_source: D'Annunzio's autograph leaflet dropped over Vienna, 9 August 1918
